🌋 Beneath the Surface: Earth’s Interior at Work

📜 Standard:
SC.7.E.6.7 – Identify and describe how Earth’s internal heat causes the movement of material within Earth and how this movement results in earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain building, and ocean basin formation.

🎯 Objective

Independently create a science-based narrative that explains how Earth’s internal heat drives movement inside the planet, resulting in changes to Earth’s surface.

Students will demonstrate understanding of internal heat, convection, and surface change through accurate science, structured storytelling, and AI image design.

🌌 Mission Briefing

Earth may appear calm on the surface, but deep beneath it is hot, active, and constantly moving. Heat from Earth’s interior causes material to rise, sink, and shift, shaping the planet over time.

 

Your mission is to explain what is happening beneath the surface and how this unseen movement leads to earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, mountain building, and ocean basin formation.

 

Your work should clearly show that Earth’s surface is shaped by forces deep inside the planet. 🌍🔥

🧰 Step 1: Choose Your Story Format

Choose ONE story format below.
No matter which option you choose, your writing must include accurate science, underlined vocabulary, and meet all assignment requirements.

🔥 Option 1: Earth’s Emergency Report

Role: Earth’s interior or mantle material
Audience: Scientists on Earth’s surface
Purpose: Explain why internal movement is occurring and what surface changes may result

 

Write a first-person emergency report warning scientists about increased activity inside Earth.

 

Your report should:

  • Explain where Earth’s internal heat comes from

  • Describe how convection currents move material inside Earth

  • Connect internal movement to at least THREE surface changes
    (earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain building, ocean basin formation)

  • Use clear cause-and-effect language

 

📡 Tone: urgent, informative, scientific.

🌋 Option 2: A Day in the Life of Magma

Role: Magma deep inside Earth
Audience: The reader
Purpose: Show how heat and movement inside Earth lead to surface change

 

Write a first-person (I, me, my), process-based narrative following magma over time. Become the Magma and explain the processes through its perspective!

 

Your story should:

  • Describe how internal heat affects density

  • Explain how convection causes magma to rise or sink

  • Show the difference between magma (below the surface) and lava (at the surface)

  • Describe at least ONE surface change you help create

 

🌡️ Tone: descriptive, process-focused, scientific.

🔬 Option 3: Mission Log: Journey Beneath the Crust

Role: Scientist exploring Earth’s interior
Audience: Research team or mission control
Purpose: Document evidence of internal movement and its effects

 

Write a scientific mission log or journal describing a journey into Earth. Think about how you are on this journey: are you sending a machine and watching on video or are you going on the journey??

 

Your log should:

  • Identify Earth’s layers

  • Describe internal heat and convection currents

  • Record observations of material movement inside Earth

  • Explain how this movement causes surface features or events

 

🧭 Tone: observational, evidence-based, professional.

🧠 Important Reminder

Your story format may change, but the science expectations do not.

 

Every option must clearly show:

Earth’s internal heat causes movement, and that movement changes Earth’s surface.

📝 Step 2: Writing Requirements

  • At least 3 paragraphs

  • Each paragraph must be 4–6 complete sentences

  • Clear cause-and-effect explanations

  • Accurate, on-topic science

🧪 Step 3: Required Science Concepts

Your story should explain:

🔥 Earth’s Internal Heat

  • Heat left from Earth’s formation

  • Heat from radioactive decay

  • How heat affects density and movement

 

🔄 Convection

  • Hot material rises

  • Cool material sinks

  • Continuous movement inside Earth

 

🌋 Surface Changes
Include and explain the following:

  • Earthquakes

  • Volcanic eruptions

  • Mountain building

  • Ocean basin formation

 

Each surface change must be directly connected to internal movement.

📚 Vocabulary

Correctly use at least 5 of the following terms in your story and underline each vocabulary word when it appears.

  • Internal heat

  • Convection

  • Mantle

  • Magma

  • Lava

  • Earthquake

  • Volcano

  • Mountain building

  • Ocean basin

 

👉 Vocabulary words only count if they are underlined and used correctly.

✍️ Step 4: Writing Format Options

Choose ONE submission format:

 

📝 Option 1: Handwritten (Science Notebook)

  • Write neatly in your science notebook

  • Take a clear, well-lit photo

  • Writing and underlines must be easy to read

 

📸 Blurry or unreadable photos will be returned for resubmission.

💻 Option 2: Typed 

  • Type your story in a Word document or Google Doc

  • Use proper paragraph formatting

  • Underline vocabulary words

  • Attach the file to the assignment

🎨 Step 5: Design a Cover Image Using AI

Create an AI-generated cover image for your story.

Your image must include:

  • The main focus of your story (Earth, magma, mantle, scientist, etc.)

  •  Each image will look different depending on which option you chose.

    • Tip: Try including a scene from your story

  • A title that matches your story

🧠 AI Prompt Example (You MUST Create Your Own)

Your AI prompt could look something like this, but it must match your story.

Your AI prompt should match your story and may be in any art style (cartoon, anime, realistic, illustrated, etc.). Remember to be specific. Describe your story and what you chose to write.

 

Example Prompt:

“A dramatic book cover showing Earth’s interior with glowing magma and convection currents beneath the crust. Volcanoes and mountains form on the surface. Earth appears powerful and active. Educational and detailed.”

📝 Step 6: Assignment Submission

Submit ALL of the following:

📄 1. Written Story
A complete narrative that meets all writing, science, and vocabulary requirements.

 

🖼️ 2. AI-Generated Cover Image

📊 Rubric

Category Points Description
🧪 Science Accuracy 10 Correct explanation of internal heat, convection, and surface changes aligned to SC.7.E.6.7
📚 Vocabulary Use 5 At least 5 vocabulary terms, correctly used and underlined
✍️ Storytelling & Explanation 10 Clear structure, strong cause-and-effect reasoning, and appropriate tone for chosen option
🎨 AI Cover Image 5 Image clearly matches the story and Earth science concepts

💯 This assignment is worth 30 points total.

🌍 Earth’s Moving Plates: A VR Plate Tectonics Report

📜 Standard:
SC.7.E.6.5– Explain the scientific theory of plate tectonics and how the movement of Earth’s crustal plates causes both slow and rapid changes in Earth’s surface.

🎯 Objective

Independently create a VR video report explaining how tectonic plates interact at a plate boundary and how that movement causes changes to Earth’s surface.

 

Students will demonstrate understanding of plate tectonics, plate movement, plate boundaries, and surface changesthrough accurate science explanations, correct vocabulary usage, and verbal communication in VR.

🌌 Mission Briefing

Earth’s surface is not fixed — it is constantly moving.

 

Beneath Earth’s crust, heat causes material in the mantle to rise and sink.
This slow movement transfers energy to Earth’s crust, causing massive tectonic plates to shift over time.

 

Although tectonic plates move only a few centimeters per year, their movement can cause:

  • Slow changes like mountain building and ocean basin formation

  • Rapid changes like earthquakes and volcanic eruptions

 

Scientists use the theory of plate tectonics to explain how these movements shape Earth’s surface.

 

Your mission is to step into virtual reality as a geologist and explain how tectonic plates interact at a boundary and how that movement causes both slow and sudden changes to Earth’s surface.

 

Your goal is to explain the process, not just name features — showing how Earth is an active, dynamic system. 🌍

🧰 Step 1: Choose Your Plate Boundary

Choose ONE type of plate boundary to focus on in your VR report:

 

⬅️➡️ Divergent Boundary
➡️⬅️ Convergent Boundary
⬆️⬇️ Transform Boundary

 

You will explain what happens when tectonic plates interact at your chosen boundary.

🎥 Step 2: VR Video Report Requirements

Record a 60–90 second VR video report explaining your chosen plate boundary.

You must clearly explain how plate movement at your boundary causes both slow and/or rapid changes to Earth’s surface.

 

Slow changes may include mountain building or ocean basin formation.
Rapid changes may include earthquakes or volcanic eruptions.

 

Your video should clearly walk through each step below. This is a spoken scientific explanation, not a script you read.

1️⃣ Explain the scientific theory of plate tectonics

Clearly explain what plate tectonics is.

 

Include:

  • What tectonic plates are

  • What layer they are part of

  • What causes them to move

2️⃣ Describe how tectonic plates move

Explain why plates move.

 

Include:

  • Heat inside Earth

  • Convection in the mantle

  • Rising and sinking material

 

Make it clear that:

  • Plates move slowly

  • Small movement can cause large changes over time

3️⃣ Explain what happens at your plate boundary

Describe how plates interact at your chosen boundary.

 

Be clear about:

  • The direction plates move

  • Whether crust is created, destroyed, or unchanged

  • What features or events may result

4️⃣ Connect plate movement to Earth’s surface changes

Explain how movement at your boundary causes changes to Earth’s surface (depending on your chosen boundary different changes are produced, make sure your change and boundary match).

Include:

  • At least ONE slow change 

  • At least ONE rapid change

 

Use cause-and-effect language such as:

  • because, as a result, over time, when…then…

⭐ Bonus Opportunity: Real-World Plate Tectonics (+2 points)

Students may earn up to 2 bonus points by including a real-world example of plate tectonics in their VR video.

 

To earn bonus points, explain:

  • A real place on Earth where your boundary type occurs

  • What changes are happening there (slow or rapid)

 

Exact names are not required — clear science reasoning matters most.

➡️ This bonus is optional and does not affect your base score.

📚 Step 3: Required Vocabulary

Correctly use at least 5 vocabulary words from the list below during your video.

  • Plate tectonics

  • Tectonic plate

  • Crust

  • Mantle

  • Plate boundary

  • Convection

  • Divergent boundary

  • Convergent boundary

  • Transform boundary

  • Earthquake

  • Volcano

 

👉 Vocabulary only counts if it is used correctly and in context.

🧠 Important Reminder

Your presentation style may vary, but the science expectations do not.

 

Every report must clearly show that:

  • Plate tectonics is a scientific theory

  • Plates move because of heat and convection

  • Plate boundaries cause both slow and rapid surface changes

🎮 Step 4: VR Environment

Choose a VR environment that helps you explain your boundary.

 

You may:

  • Point to land features

  • Use gestures to show plate movement

  • Walk through the environment while explaining

 

The environment does not need to be exact— your scientific explanation is what matters most.

📝 Step 5: Assignment Submission

Submit ALL of the following:

🎥 1. VR Video Report (2D Video Only)
A clear, complete explanation that meets all science and vocabulary requirements.

 

⚠️ Important Reminder:
Your submission must be a 2D video recording, not a spatial recording.

💡 Quick Tip (Read Before Submitting)

If you accidentally record a spatial recording and need to resubmit:

  • Load your spatial recording

  • Play it back

  • Then take a 2D video of your recording while it plays

 

This allows you to submit the correct format without re-recording your entire presentation.

📊 Rubric

Category Points Description
🧪 Science Accuracy 10 Correct explanation of plate boundaries and plate movement
📚 Vocabulary Use 5 At least 5 terms used correctly
🎤 Clarity & Explanation 10 Clear, organized, cause-and-effect reasoning
🎮 VR Engagement 5 On-task use of VR to support explanation
Total 30 points

⭐ Bonus: Up to +2 points for a clear, accurate real-world example connected to plate movement.

💯 This assignment is worth 30 points total, with up to 2 bonus points available.

📰 OPTIMA Times: Plate Tectonics in Motion Special Issue

Breaking News: Earth’s Surface Is Shifting — and You’re Reporting the Impact!

📜 Standard:
SC.7.E.6.5– Explain the scientific theory of plate tectonics and how the movement of Earth’s crustal plates causes both slow and rapid changes in Earth’s surface.

🎯 Objective

Use AI tools and Canva to design a science magazine cover for The OPTIMA Times that explains how tectonic plate movement causes changes to Earth’s surface.

 

Your mission: report on Earth’s powerful internal forces like a science journalist, using visuals and headlines to explain real scientific processes.

💬 Essential Question

“How does plate movement cause both sudden and slow changes to Earth’s surface?”

🧠 Mission Briefing

Breaking news from deep beneath Earth’s surface, Science Correspondent! 🌍

 

Earth’s surface may seem solid and unchanging, but massive tectonic plates are constantly moving beneath our feet. Driven by heat inside Earth, these plates shift slowly over time — building mountains and ocean basins — and sometimes release energy suddenly, causing earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.

 

Scientists use the theory of plate tectonics to explain:

  • Why earthquakes shake the ground

  • How volcanoes create new land

  • Why mountains take millions of years to form

  • How ocean basins expand over time

 

Your assignment is to investigate one major surface change caused by plate movement and report on it for a special issue of The OPTIMA Times.

 

You are both the scientist and the journalist — explaining how Earth’s internal motion shapes the planet we live on.

🧩 Assignment Steps

1️⃣ Choose Your Plate Movement Topic

Select ONE Earth surface change caused by plate movement:

🌎 Earthquake
🌋 Volcano
⛰️ Mountain Building
🌊 Ocean Basin Formation

 

You will focus your magazine cover on explaining how plate movement causes this change.

2️⃣ Generate Your Visual

Use an AI image generator to create a clear, accurate visual showing your chosen plate-related change.

 

Your image must:

  • Clearly show the event or landform

  • Represent plate movement or its effects

  • Look appropriate for a science magazine

  • Leave space for headlines and text

 

This image will be the main cover photo of your magazine.

3️⃣ Design Your Magazine Cover in Canva

Go to Canva and search for magazine cover template.

 

Choose a layout that fits a science or news magazine.

 

Your cover must include:

  • 📰 Magazine Title: OPTIMA Times

  • 🗞️ Main Headline about your plate movement topic

  • 📝 A supporting headline and blurbs

  • 🖼️ Your AI-generated image as the background

 

Your final product should look like a real magazine cover, not a poster or slideshow.
Take a look at my example Magazine cover about Volcanos!!

4️⃣ Science Content Requirements

Your magazine cover text must clearly explain:

  • What is happening (earthquake, volcano, etc.)

  • How plate movement causes this change

  • Whether the change happens quickly or slowly

 

Your explanations should reflect the theory of plate tectonics, even if the phrase is not used directly.

🧠 Important Reminder

Your design style may vary — but the science expectations do not.

 

Every magazine cover must clearly show that:

  • Heat inside Earth causes plate movement

  • Plate movement creates stress or pressure

  • Some surface changes happen suddenly

  • Other surface changes take millions of years

📤 Submit Your Work

Submit the of the following:

🖼️ 1. Final Magazine Cover Image
Downloaded as a PNG or JPG (no links).

 

⚠️ Links will not be accepted. Files must be uploaded to receive full credit.

📊 Rubric

Category Points Description
🧪 Science Accuracy 5 Correct explanation of how plate movement causes the surface change
📰 Magazine Design 5 Clear, organized, magazine-style layout
Total 10 points

 

💯 This assignment is worth 10 points total.

🌍 Plate Boundaries in Action: 3D Pen Earth Science Model
A Hands-On Tectonics Construction Challenge

📜 Standard:
SC.7.E.6.5 – Explore the scientific theory of plate tectonics by describing how the movement of Earth’s crustal plates causes both slow and rapid changes in Earth’s surface, including volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, and mountain building.

🎯 Objective
Create a 3D pen model in VR that demonstrates how plate boundaries cause specific changes to Earth’s surface.

 

You will:

• Choose ONE type of plate boundary
• Show how the plates move
• Show what feature or event forms because of that movement

💬 Essential Question
How does the movement of tectonic plates at different boundaries create different features and events on Earth?

🧠 Mission Briefing

Earth’s surface may look solid and still — but it is not.

 

Deep below our feet, giant pieces of Earth’s crust called tectonic plates are constantly moving. Where these plates meet, they form plate boundaries.


There are three main types of boundaries:

• Divergent – plates move apart
• Convergent – plates move toward each other
• Transform – plates slide past each other

 

These movements can create:

🪨 The Rock That Refused to Stay the Same

An OPTIMA Science Comic Special Issue

📜 Standard:

SC.7.E.6.2 – Identify and describe the processes involved in the rock cycle and how surface and sub-surface processes change rocks from one type to another.

🎯 Objective

Independently create a hand-drawn science comic telling the life story of ONE type of rock and explaining:

  • How it forms

  • What processes create it

  • What makes it unique

  • How it can change into other rock types over time through the rock cycle

Students will demonstrate understanding of rock formation, rock cycle processes, and surface and sub-surface changes through accurate science explanations, correct vocabulary usage, and clear visual storytelling.

🌌 Mission Briefing

Some rocks are born in fire.

Some are pressed deep underground under crushing pressure.

Some are broken into tiny pieces by wind, water, and time — then slowly rebuilt into something new.

And some refuse to stay the same for very long.

 

At first glance, rocks seem like the most unchanging things on Earth. They sit quietly in mountains, on beaches, and beneath our feet. They don’t move. They don’t grow. They don’t appear to change.

 

But that is only what we see on the surface.

 

Deep inside Earth and all across its surface, rocks are constantly changing.

 

They melt in Earth’s heat and cool into new forms.
They are squeezed by pressure until their structure changes.
They are broken apart by weather and water, carried away, and slowly turned into something new.

 

Over millions of years, the same material is:

  • Melted

  • Reformed

  • Broken

  • Compressed

  • Rebuilt

Again and again.

 

This never-ending system is called the rock cycle.

There is no beginning and no end — only continuous change.

 

A rock that starts as one type may not stay that way forever. Given enough time and the right conditions, it can become something completely different.

 

Your mission is to tell the life story of one rock — a rock that refuses to stay the same.

 

You will show:

  • How it was born

  • What processes shaped it

  • How it changed over time

  • And how it could become something new in the future

 

Your goal is to explain the process, not just name facts — to show that Earth is not a static planet, but a living, changing system powered by heat, pressure, water, and time. 🌍

🧰 Step 1: Choose Your Rock Type

  • 🌋 Igneous

  • 🏞️ Sedimentary

  • 🔥 Metamorphic

Your 2-page comic must focus deeply on ONE rock type and include:

🔹 If You Choose 🌋 IGNEOUS:

  • It forms when magma or lava cools and hardens

  • It can form:

    • Below the surface (magma)

    • At the surface (lava)

  • It is created by heat deep inside Earth

  • You must show or explain:

    • Melting

    • Cooling

🔹 If You Choose 🏞️ SEDIMENTARY:

Your comic must show that:

  • It forms from sediment

  • Sediment comes from:

    • Broken pieces of rock

    • Sand, soil, or shells

  • You must show the FULL process:

    • Weathering (breaks rock)

    • Erosion (moves sediment)

    • Deposition (drops sediment)

    • Compaction and cementation (turn sediment into rock)

  • You should show:

    • Sedimentary rocks often form in layers

🔹 If You Choose 🔥 METAMORPHIC:

Your comic must show that:

  • It forms when existing rock is changed by heat and pressure

  • The rock:

    • Does NOT melt

    • Becomes harder and denser

  • This happens deep underground

  • You must show or explain:

    • Heat

    • Pressure

    • That the rock is changed, not destroyed

🔁 Step 4: Show How Your Rock Can Change

Your comic must ALSO show:

  • How your rock could eventually change into a different rock type

  • What process would cause that change (heat, pressure, weathering, erosion, melting, etc.)

🌎 Mission Briefing

  • At the surface (weathering, erosion, deposition)

  • Below the surface (plate tectonics, heat, pressure, mountain building)

Subsurface Processes

🥼 Demonstration Station: Measuring the Age of Earth

📜 Standard:
SC.7.E.6.3 – Describe how relative dating and radioactive dating methods are used to determine the age of rocks and fossils.

🎯 Objective
Independently create a demonstration scene that shows how scientists determine the age of Earth materials using relative dating and/or absolute (radioactive) dating.

 

Through this task, students will model how scientists use evidence from rocks and materials to determine age over geologic time. Students will demonstrate understanding by building, labeling, and explaining dating methods using visual models and in-world sticky notes rather than written paragraphs.

 

This assignment is designed to move students beyond memorizing definitions and toward understanding how scientists know what they know about Earth’s history. By the end of this activity, students should be able to show how rock position, radioactive decay, and half-life provide evidence for Earth’s age.

🌌 Mission Briefing
Earth is about 4.6 billion years old, but scientists cannot measure its age directly.

 

Instead, scientists study rocks, fossils, and Earth materials to determine age using evidence.

 

There are two main methods scientists use:

  • Relative dating, which compares what is older or younger

  • Absolute dating, which determines an actual numerical age

 

These methods allow scientists to reconstruct Earth’s history across geologic time.

 

Your mission is to step into virtual reality as a geologic investigator and enter the Demonstration Station.

 

You will build, label, and explain how scientists measure age using rock layers, radioactive elements, and predictable decay patterns.

 

Your goal is not just to name dating methods, but to demonstrate how evidence is used to determine Earth’s age. ⏳🌍

🧰 Step 1: Choose Your Dating Method to Demonstrate
Choose ONE method to demonstrate, or combine both for a more advanced model.

🧱 Relative Dating (Law of Superposition)

Relative dating determines whether materials are older or younger than others.

 

Key ideas you may model:

  • Rock layers stacked on top of each other

  • Older layers on the bottom

  • Younger layers on the top

  • Undisturbed sedimentary rock layers

 

Examples:

  • A stack of sedimentary layers

  • Fossils found in lower vs. higher layers

  • Showing which layer formed first

🧬 Absolute Dating (Radioactive Dating)

Absolute dating determines the actual age of materials in years.

 

Key ideas you may model:

  • Radioactive elements inside rocks

  • Radioactive decay over time

🎨 Earth Evidence Studio: Infographic Poster Project

 

📜 Standard:
SC.7.E.6.4 – Explain how evidence of physical changes in Earth’s surface supports scientific theories of Earth’s evolution over geologic time.

🎯 Objective
Independently create an infographic-style poster that visually explains how scientists use physical evidence to understand how Earth has changed over geologic time.

 

Through this task, you will communicate scientific ideas using diagrams, layout, visuals, and concise explanations rather than long written responses. Scientists often use visual models and evidence displays to communicate complex Earth science concepts, and this assignment focuses on building those same scientific communication skills.

 

This assignment is designed to move you beyond simply identifying evidence and toward explaining how that evidence supports scientific theories about Earth’s history. By the end of this activity, you should be able to clearly show how scientists use physical evidence to explain Earth’s changing surface.

🌌 Mission Briefing
Earth has not always looked the way it does today.

 

Mountains have formed and worn down, oceans have opened and closed, continents have shifted, climates have changed, and life on Earth has evolved over millions and billions of years.

 

Because most of these changes occur over geologic time — extremely long periods far beyond a human lifetime — scientists rely on physical evidence preserved in rocks, fossils, landforms, and Earth’s surface features.

 

This evidence helps scientists develop scientific theories explaining how Earth has changed through natural processes like plate tectonics, weathering and erosion, volcanic activity, and sediment deposition.

 

Your mission is to enter the Earth Evidence Studio and design an educational infographic poster that clearly shows how one type of physical evidence supports scientific explanations of Earth’s change over time.

 

Your goal is not just to name evidence, but to show how scientists interpret it to understand Earth’s history.

🎨 Step 1: Choose ONE Evidence Focus

Select ONE type of evidence showing how Earth has changed over geologic time. Your entire infographic poster will focus on explaining this evidence and how scientists use it.

 

Below are detailed options to help guide your choice:

🪨 Rock Layers / Geologic Evidence
Focus on how rock layers record Earth’s history.

 

You might show:

• Sedimentary rock layers stacked over time
• Older layers below, younger layers above
• Evidence of past environments (oceans, deserts, forests)
• Volcanic ash layers or lava flows between rock layers
• Folded, faulted, or tilted rock layers

 

This option works well if you enjoy geology, Earth history, or visual diagrams.

🦴 Fossils / Evidence of Past Life
Focus on how fossils show changes in organisms and environments over time.

 

You might show:

• Fossils found in rock layers
• Different fossils in different layers
• Marine fossils found on land
• Changes in organism types over time
• Evidence of extinction

 

This option connects Earth science with life science concepts.

🌍 Landforms as Evidence
Focus on large surface features shaped over long periods.

 

You might show:

• Mountains formed by plate movement
• Canyons created by erosion
• Volcanoes and lava flows
• Ocean basins or mid-ocean ridges
• Glacial landforms

 

This option works well if you like surface processes and physical geography.

🧩 Continental Evidence
Focus on how continents have moved over time.

 

You might show:

• Continents fitting together like puzzle pieces
• Matching fossils across continents
• Similar rock types on separate continents
• Evidence supporting continental drift
• Plate tectonic movement

 

This option highlights large-scale Earth system changes.

🌋 Natural Processes Evidence
Focus on processes that actively change Earth.

 

You might show:

• Plate tectonic movement
• Earthquakes and fault lines
• Volcanic eruptions and lava deposits
• Weathering and erosion
• Sediment deposition over time

 

This option emphasizes ongoing Earth change.

👉 Choose the evidence type you feel most confident explaining.
Your goal is to clearly show how scientists use this evidence to understand Earth’s history — not just identify it.

🧠 Step 2: Poster Requirements

Your poster MUST include ALL of the following:

 

📊 Visual Diagram or Illustration
Clear drawing, labeled diagram, or digital graphic showing the evidence.

 

➡️ Evidence Indicators
Arrows, labels, or visual cues showing what scientists observe.

 

🏷️ Clear Labels
Identify the evidence type and important features.

 

📝 Explanation (2–4 sentences recommended)
Explain:

• What the evidence shows
• What change occurred over time
• How scientists use this evidence to support a scientific theory

 

🌍 Real Example
Include a real-world example (specific fossil, landform, rock formation, tectonic feature, etc.).

 

👉 Tip: Strong vocabulary helps. Consider terms like geologic time, sedimentary layers, fossils, erosion, continental drift, plate tectonics, volcanic activity, physical evidence, or scientific theory.

🎮 Step 3: Design Format

Poster may be created:

• Digitally (Canva, Google Slides, drawing apps, etc.)
• Hand drawn and photographed for submission

 

Focus on:

• Clear organization
• Readable text
• Logical layout
• Accurate science content
• Visual clarity

 

Remember: this is scientific communication. Someone should learn from your poster without additional explanation.

📝 Step 4: Assignment Submission

Submit ONE completed poster.

 

Your submission should clearly show:

• The evidence example
• Labels and explanations
• Connection to Earth’s change over time
• Scientific reasoning

 

If submitting hand drawn:

• Good lighting
• Clear text
• Avoid blur
• Crop distractions if needed

 

Clear visuals strengthen scientific communication.

📊 Rubric

Category Points What This Means
🧪 Required Scientific Content 10 Poster clearly explains one type of Earth evidence and how it supports scientific theories of Earth’s change over time.
🏷️ Visual Elements & Labels 5 Poster includes diagram, labels, real-world example, and clear evidence indicators.
🔍 Scientific Communication 5 Poster is organized, readable, visually clear, and effectively communicates scientific evidence.

📜 Standard:
SC.7.E.6.6 – Describe ways in which human activity has an impact on the atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, geosphere, and biosphere.

🎯 Objective

In this assignment, you will take on the role of an environmental field scientist investigating a damaged ecosystem.

 

You will:

  • Describe how a healthy ecosystem should function

  • Analyze how human activity disrupted Earth’s systems

You have arrived at a site where an ecosystem has been severely damaged by human activity.

 

Your task is to document:

  • What this environment should look like in its natural state

  • What human activity occurred

  • How each Earth sphere was affected

  • Must include labels for at least two Earth spheres

  • Should clearly show visible differences

 

The primary focus of this assignment is your written scientific analysis.

Take a well-lit, clear photograph of your completed notebook page(s).

 

Your image must:

In Part 2 of Impact Zone: Disrupting Earth’s Balance, you will apply your understanding of Earth’s interconnected systems to analyze how human activity can destabilize a previously balanced ecosystem.

 

Using the SAME forest or coral reef ecosystem you constructed in Part 1, you will introduce a specific human activity and demonstrate how that action alters the geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere, and cryosphere.

  • Demonstrate how matter and energy movement is altered.

  • Predict long-term ecosystem outcomes.

This assignment requires systems thinking. When humans alter one part of Earth’s system, the effects rarely stay isolated.

 

By the end of this assignment, you should be able to clearly demonstrate that:

  • Human actions can disrupt ecological balance.

  • Environmental change spreads from one sphere to others.

  • Local human decisions can have broader environmental consequences.

  • Responsible environmental choices matter.

🌌 Mission Briefing

Last week, you demonstrated how Earth’s spheres work together in balance.

 

Forests regulate temperature, stabilize soil, and support biodiversity.
Coral reefs protect coastlines, support marine food webs, and depend on sunlight and clean water.

 

This week, you will explore what happens when human actions disrupt that balance.

Human activity has the power to reshape Earth’s systems.

 

You will choose one of the following:

🌲 Deforestation
🏙️ Urbanization
🏜️ Desertification
💧 Water Pollution
🚰 Dam Construction

🌲 Deforestation

In a Forest Ecosystem:

  • Trees (biosphere) are removed.

  • Soil (geosphere) becomes exposed and vulnerable to erosion.

  • Rainwater (hydrosphere) runs off more quickly.

  • Sediment may enter rivers.

  • Atmospheric carbon dioxide may increase.

  • Habitat loss reduces biodiversity.

 

In a Coral Reef Ecosystem:

  • Coastal tree removal increases sediment runoff.

  • Sediment clouds ocean water (hydrosphere).

  • Chemicals or waste enter ocean water.

  • River flow changes.

  • Sediment movement is altered.

  • Migration patterns shift.

 

In a Coral Reef Ecosystem:

  • Freshwater flow changes ocean salinity.

🔥 Particle Motion Lab: Build a State of Matter Model


📜 Standard:
SC.7.P.11.1 – Recognize that adding heat to or removing heat from a system may result in a temperature change and possibly a change of state.

🎯 Objective
In this investigation, you will build a 3D physical model that shows how heat affects particle motion and the states of matter.

 

Scientists often use models to help visualize how particles behave in solids, liquids, and gases. Because particles are too small to see directly, models help us understand how heat energy changes the movement of particles.

 

Your model will help demonstrate:

• How heat affects particle motion
• The difference between solid, liquid, and gas particle movement
• How adding or removing heat can change the state of matter

 

By the end of this assignment, you should be able to:

• Represent particle motion in solids, liquids, and gases
• Show how adding heat increases particle movement
• Show how removing heat decreases particle movement
• Identify examples of changes of state

🔥 Mission Briefing

ALL matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving.

The amount of motion depends on how much heat energy is present.

 

When heat is added or removed, particles move differently.

 

In a solid, particles vibrate in place and stay tightly packed together.

In a liquid, particles still stay close together but can slide past each other.

In a gas, particles move quickly and spread far apart.

 

Heat energy changes how particles move, and this motion determines the state of matter.

When enough heat is added or removed, matter can change state.

 

Examples include:

• Evaporation / Boiling – liquid → gas
• Condensation – gas → liquid
• Freezing – liquid → solid

 

Scientists use particle models to explain these changes.

 

Your mission is to build a particle motion model that shows how heat affects the states of matter.

🧰 Your Task

Using materials you can find around your house, build a 3D particle motion model that shows the three states of matter.

 

⚠️ This assignment MUST be a 3D physical model made with materials.
It should NOT be a drawing or diagram on paper.

 

Your model should show:

• Particles in a solid
• Particles in a liquid
• Particles in a gas

 

You may use materials such as:

• Beads or small balls
• Clay or playdough
• Rice or beans
• Cotton balls
• Bottle caps or small objects
• Cardboard or containers
• Recycled materials

 

Your materials should clearly represent particles and how they move in each state of matter.

⭐ What Your Model Must Show

Your model must include three sections representing the states of matter.

 

🧊 Solid

Show:

• Particles packed closely together
• Very little space between particles
• Particles vibrating in place

 

Label and explain:

• Low particle motion
• Low energy

💧 Liquid

Show:

• Particles still close together

🔥➡️❄️ Heat Transfer Mission: Restore Thermal Equilibrium

📜 Standard:
SC.7.P.11.4 – Observe and describe that heat flows in predictable ways, moving from warmer objects to cooler ones until they reach the same temperature.

🎯 Objective

In this assignment, you will build a VR model that demonstrates heat transfer and thermal equilibrium.

Heat is a form of energy that moves between things when there is a temperature difference. Heat always moves in a predictable direction: from warmer to cooler.

 

This movement happens because particles in warmer materials move faster than particles in cooler materials. When they interact, the faster-moving particles transfer energy to the slower-moving particles.

 

As energy transfers, temperatures begin to change. The warmer item cools down while the cooler item warms up.

 

Eventually, both reach the same temperature. When this happens, heat transfer stops. This state is called thermal equilibrium.

 

In this activity, you will use VR modeling to demonstrate how heat moves and how balance is eventually reached.

 

By the end of this assignment, you should be able to:

Explain the direction of heat transfer

Model how heat moves from warmer to cooler

🌌 Mission Briefing

Your VR simulation has detected an energy imbalance.

 

Two things in your environment have very different temperatures. One is much warmer, while the other is much cooler. Because of this difference, energy immediately begins to move.

 

Heat always flows in one direction:

Warm → Cool

 

As heat transfers:

• The warmer item begins to cool down
• The cooler item begins to warm up

 

This process continues until both reach the same temperature.

When this happens, the system reaches thermal equilibrium.

 

At equilibrium:

• Heat is no longer transferring between them
• Temperatures are equal
• The system becomes balanced

 

Your mission is to build a VR environment that clearly demonstrates how heat moves and how equilibrium is restored.

 

Anyone exploring your world should be able to clearly see how heat travels from warmer to cooler areas and how balance is eventually reached.

📜 Standard:

SC.7.P.11.3- Cite evidence to explain that energy cannot be created nor destroyed, only changed from one form to another.

🎯 Objective

In this assignment, you will create a VR breaking news broadcast explaining the Law of Conservation of Energy.

 

Energy is involved in nearly every change that occurs in the universe. Whenever something moves, produces heat, gives off light, or creates sound, energy is involved.

Energy can exist in many forms, including thermal energy, light energy, sound energy, electrical energy, chemical energy, and mechanical energy. These different forms of energy can change from one form into another through processes called energy transformations.

 

Scientists have discovered an important rule about energy called the Law of Conservation of Energy. This law states that energy cannot be created or destroyed. Instead, energy can only be transferred from one object to another or transformed from one form into another.

 

Even when energy seems to disappear, it has actually changed form or moved somewhere else in the system.

For example, when a flashlight turns on, chemical energy stored in the battery changes into electrical energy, which then produces light and heat. The energy was not created—it simply changed form.

 

By studying how energy moves and changes forms, scientists can better understand how systems work.

In this assignment, you will act as a news reporter inside a VR news studio and produce a short breaking news broadcast explaining how the Law of Conservation of Energy works in real-world situations.

 

By the end of this assignment, you should be able to:

• Define energy as the ability to cause change or do work
• Explain the Law of Conservation of Energy
• Identify examples of energy transfer
• Identify examples of energy transformation

🌌 Mission Briefing

Scientists have confirmed an important discovery about how energy behaves.

 

According to the Law of Conservation of Energy, energy cannot be created or destroyed. Instead, energy can only move between objects or change from one form into another.

This means the total amount of energy in a system remains constant, even when energy transformations occur.

 

For example, when a moving object slows down, it may seem like the energy of motion has disappeared. In reality, some of that energy has been transformed into thermal energy due to friction.

 

Other systems show similar transformations. Electrical energy can become light and heat in a light bulb. Chemical energy in food can be transformed into mechanical energy when muscles move.

Scientists track these changes to observe how energy moves through systems.

 

Your mission is to report on this scientific discovery as a breaking news broadcast explaining how the Law of Conservation of Energy works in real-world systems.

🧠 Putting AI to the Test: Energy Transformations

📜 Standard:
SC.7.P.11.3 – Recognize that energy can be transformed from one form to another, including electrical, mechanical, chemical, thermal, and radiant energy.

🎯 Objective

In this assignment, you will use an AI image generator to create a scientific diagram showing how energy transforms from one form into another within a system.

 

Energy is constantly changing form in the world around us. Every time something moves, produces heat, gives off light, or creates sound, energy is being transferred or transformed.

 

Scientists explain this principle using the Law of Conservation of Energy, which states that energy cannot be created or destroyed. Instead, energy can move between objects or change from one form into another.

 

Because energy transformations occur in nearly every physical process, scientists often study how energy moves through systems and what evidence shows that energy is conserved.

 

Examples of common energy transformations include:

• A flashlight converting chemical energy → electrical energy → light and thermal energy
• A toaster converting electrical energy → thermal energy
• A car converting chemical energy in fuel → mechanical energy
• A speaker converting electrical energy → sound energy

 

In each of these examples, the energy does not disappear. Instead, it changes form while the total amount of energy in the system remains constant.

 

In this assignment, you will put AI to the test by generating a visual model of an energy transformation system and evaluating how accurately the AI represents the science.

 

By the end of this assignment, you should be able to:

• Identify different forms of energy

• Evaluate whether an AI-generated scientific diagram accurately represents energy transformations

🌌 Mission Briefing

Scientists often study energy by examining systems, which are the objects or processes being investigated.

 

When scientists analyze a system, they track:

• The initial form of energy
• The energy transformations that occur
• The final forms of energy produced

 

Sometimes these final forms include heat, sound, light, or motion, which serve as evidence that energy has changed form rather than disappeared.

 

Your mission is to use AI as a scientific tool to generate a diagram showing how energy moves through a system. Then you will evaluate the results and determine whether the AI correctly represented the energy transformations.

AI tools often generate very similar images when the same prompt is used, which makes it easy to identify copied prompts. If the same prompt is used, the images will look nearly identical and it will be clear that the example prompt was used.

Students will demonstrate understanding of how solar energy is transferred through space as waves by accurately modeling radiation, wavelength, and different types of electromagnetic energy using correct scientific vocabulary and clear cause-and-effect explanations.

Infrared radiation warms Earth’s surface.

assignments.html:
💡Light Lab: Investigating How Light Interacts with Matter

📜 Standard:
SC.7.P.10.2 – Observe and explain that light can be reflected, refracted, and/or absorbed.

🎯 Objective

In this assignment, you will step into the role of a scientist and design a working lab model in VR that demonstrates how light interacts with different materials.

Light is a form of energy that travels in waves and interacts with objects in different ways.

 

When light hits an object, it can:
• Reflect (bounce off)
• Refract (bend through)
• Absorb (turn into heat)

These interactions explain how we see, how lenses work, and how energy is transferred through light.

 

By the end of this assignment, you should be able to:

• Explain how light interacts with matter
• Identify reflection, refraction, and absorption
• Design a scientific model that demonstrates light behavior
• Use evidence and reasoning to explain what happens to light

🔦 Mission Briefing

The lab lights flicker.

A sharp beam of light cuts across the room—then bends, scatters, and vanishes into darkness.

 

Your console crackles to life.

“…Light Behavior Analysis Unit… do you copy…”

 

The signal distorts, then stabilizes.

“We are losing control of our optical systems.”

 

Data floods your screen—light beams refracting unpredictably, reflections scattering in the wrong directions, energy readings spiking where absorption should not be occurring.

A second transmission overrides the first.

 

Critical technologies are beginning to fail:

• Imaging systems cannot focus
• Communication signals are breaking apart
• Energy systems are overheating
• Measurement tools are returning inconsistent data

 

Scientists rely on light to observe, measure, and understand the world. But right now, light is not behaving as expected—and no one knows why.

 

Without understanding how light interacts with different materials:

• Observations cannot be trusted
• Data cannot be confirmed
• Systems cannot be repaired

 

You have been selected as part of the Light Interaction Research Team.

Your mission is to design a controlled lab model that allows scientists to observe exactly how light behaves when it reflects, refracts, and absorbs across different materials.

 

Every section of your lab must reveal what is happening to the light—and why.

 

The signal cuts out.

The room goes quiet.

 

A single beam of light powers on in front of you.

The lab is ready.

🧪 Lab Environment

For this assignment:

➡️ Enter one of the Science Lab environments in ENGAGE VR

These spaces are designed for:
• Controlled experiments
• Clear observation setups
• Organized scientific modeling

 

➡️ Build your model on a lab workstation or table

 

Your build should feel like:
• A scientific model
• A controlled experiment setup
• A tabletop investigation, not a full environment

 

💡 Mission Reminder
Great scientists don’t just observe the world—they design experiments to understand it.

Now it’s your turn. 🧪

🧰 Your Task

You will design and build a light investigation lab setup in VR that allows scientists to observe and test how light interacts with different materials.

 

Your build should stay contained to a lab table or workstation-sized space—not a full room or large environment.

 

Think of your build as a working experiment, not just a model. A scientist should be able to look at your lab and clearly understand how light is behaving in each section. They should be able to predict what will happen to the light before it even reaches each material.

💡 Understanding Light Interactions (Examples)

Before you build, make sure you understand what each interaction looks like:

• Reflection (light bounces off a surface)
Example: Light hitting a mirror and bouncing back, allowing you to see your reflection

• Refraction (light bends when passing through a material)
Example: A straw appearing bent in a glass of water, or light passing through a lens

• Absorption (light energy is taken in and often converted into heat)
Example: Black pavement getting hot in the sun because it absorbs light energy

Your goal is to create a space where light can be:
• Directed toward different materials
• Observed as it changes direction or energy
• Compared across different surfaces

Before you begin building, think like a scientist:

• Where will your light source be placed?
• What materials will the light interact with?
• How will you clearly show what happens to the light?
• How will someone observing your lab understand each interaction?

Your lab MUST include:

• A section that clearly demonstrates reflection
• A section that clearly demonstrates refraction
• A section that clearly demonstrates absorption
• At least two different types of materials (transparent, translucent, or opaque)
• A visible path showing how light travels (arrows, beams, etc.)

Your design should:

• Stay within a contained tabletop/workstation space
• Be organized into clear sections (like real lab stations)
• Show cause and effect
• Allow someone to follow the light from start to finish
• Make it easy to compare how light behaves

 

If your lab works correctly, you should be able to explain every change in the light from start to finish.

At the end of your build, your lab should answer:

“How does light change when it interacts with different materials?”

Step 1— Enter VR

1️⃣ Enter ENGAGE VR
2️⃣ Enter the assigned VR space
3️⃣ Change your Group to: OAO Grade 7

 

🔬 Enter a Science Lab environment with workstations

 

Explore Public IFX for:
• Light sources
• Glass or transparent materials
• Reflective surfaces

Step 2— Design Your Lab Setup

Inside VR, you will:

• Build your model on a table or workstation
• Create separate areas for each type of light interaction
• Use objects to represent mirrors, lenses, and materials
• Show the path of light using arrows, beams, or direction indicators

 

Your lab should feel like a real experiment in progress.

Step 3— Sticky Note Explanations

You MUST use sticky notes in VR.

 

Your sticky notes must include:

• Name of your lab setup
• Where reflection occurs and what is happening
• Where refraction occurs and why light bends
• Where absorption occurs and what happens to energy
• Types of materials used
• What happens to light in each section
• A real-world connection (glasses, mirrors, sunlight, etc.)

Step 4— Scientific Thinking

Your lab must show that you understand:

• Light can change direction or energy, not disappear
• Materials determine how light behaves
• Multiple interactions can occur at the same time

 

This is not just a build. It is a scientific investigation.

🌎 Required Components

✔ Tabletop lab model
✔ Clearly labeled sections
✔ Sticky note explanations
✔ Clear demonstration of light interactions

📸 Submission Requirement— Pictures

You must upload:

• Multiple pictures of your lab
• Clear images of sticky notes
• Angles that show light movement

 

Your pictures must clearly show both your experiment AND your explanations.

📊 Rubric

SC.7.P.10.3 – Describe how waves can transfer energy through a medium.

🎯 Objective

In this assignment, you will step into the role of a designer and create your own educational theme park based on how waves move through different materials.

Waves are all around us and are responsible for many everyday experiences, including sound, light, and motion in water.

 

Because waves behave differently depending on the material they travel through:

• Some waves move faster in solids than in liquids or gases
• Light waves can travel through empty space, but sound waves cannot
• Waves transfer energy, not matter
• The medium affects how waves move and behave

 

By the end of this assignment, you should be able to:

• Explain how waves move through different materials
• Connect science to real-world applications
• Describe how energy moves through waves
• Communicate ideas clearly through writing

🌊 Mission Briefing
